question: Why can an English contract still be made binding by a single peppercorn?
answer: Because English courts ask whether something was given in exchange, not whether it was worth enough. In 1959, in Chappell v Nestlé, the House of Lords held that chocolate wrappers binned on receipt counted, and remarked that a peppercorn stays good payment to someone who dislikes pepper. Leases still charge one peppercorn a year.
move: A court that refuses to weigh a price leaves the bargain to the bargainers.
ask: When two people strike a deal, do I let them set the price or judge it for them?
source: Chappell v Nestlé, House of Lords, 1960
reference: Chappell & Co Ltd v Nestlé Co Ltd, House of Lords, [1960] AC 87, 1959
